finding: §2 changes `clean` without noticing that the shipped `divergence` signal is built on the equivalence it breaks, and the inversion silences the signal exactly where `blocking` makes it decision-relevant. `engine.ComputeAuditDivergence` (internal/engine/divergence.go:95-127) emits only when five conditions hold, of which 4 is 'the sequence is not converged', and its own doc comment states the premise: "Condition 4 is redundant in every sane configuration, since condition 2 makes the latest round unclean and that is what convergence counts." Under `blocking` condition 2 (a non-`PASS` row not attributed to spec-coverage) no longer makes the round unclean — a `warning` row leaves `clean: true` — so condition 4 stops being redundant and starts SUPPRESSING the object on precisely the state the release creates: spec-coverage clean, other roles open at advisory severity, gate open. Where the sequence is not yet converged the object is emitted but `next_action` now takes the 'run the next audit round' branch instead of the fix-and-re-audit directive, falsifying REFERENCE.md:883-885 ("Whenever `divergence` is emitted over state tp itself recorded, `next_action` reads the fix-and-re-audit directive"). §2 enumerates the surfaces that stay severity-blind and `divergence` is not among them; §6's Non-Goal 1 defers only the `--check` role-scoping divergence, which is a different subject.
suggestion: Decide `divergence`'s behaviour under `blocking` in §2 beside `next_action`: either condition 4 is re-stated over the severity-blind non-`PASS` count so the object survives a clean-under-blocking round, or the release states that `divergence` is withheld once the gate opens and says why. Add it to the enumerated list of `clean` consumers, and give it a §7 row.

finding: §3 states the fence unconditionally and §7 test 12 silently narrows it, so the release as specified ships a knob nobody can set and §7 holds no row that would notice. §3's normative sentence is 'The fence refuses a write that CHANGES the resolved value to blocking', with no attended/unattended distinction anywhere in the section -- a regex search for 'unattended|UNATTENDED|tp run' over spec/0.37.0.md returns exactly four lines (140, 141, 149 and test row 278) and none is a scoping clause. Test 12 introduces TP_UNATTENDED=1 for the first time, as a test condition rather than as a rule. Read literally, §3 refuses every write of blocking including the operator's, which makes §1's deliverable 1 unreachable; read via test 12, the fence is inert without the variable, and no row asserts that an attended write of blocking succeeds and resolves. §3's own table argues for the narrow reading without stating it: row 1's tp import deadlock is qualified 'under tp run', which is only a deadlock if attended imports pass. Wrong if: §3 named TP_UNATTENDED as the condition, and §7 carried the attended-path row.
suggestion: Add to §3 immediately after the change-rule sentence: 'The refusal is the unattended fence: it fires when TP_UNATTENDED is set, on the same terms as the four decisions already reserved for the operator. Attended, the same write succeeds -- that is what makes the field opt-in rather than absent.' Then add row 12b: '| 12b | §3 *the fence* | with TP_UNATTENDED unset, a write of blocking on each of the three paths exits 0 and the field resolves to blocking -- three assertions | a fence that refuses unconditionally, which ships an unsettable knob and passes test 12 |'.

finding: §3's "resolved, not stored" paragraph mandates a refusal for a case that cannot occur under §2's stated precedence, and misses the one write that CAN produce it. §3 requires: "a --project write of `all` that *uncovers* a task override of `blocking` changes the resolved value and must be refused." Under §2's precedence (task override > project config > built-in) a task override of blocking already wins, so writing anything at the project layer leaves the resolved value at blocking -- no change, nothing to refuse -- and neither setter has an unset form (read internal/cli/set.go:325-506 and internal/cli/set_project.go:22-120: every branch assigns a value; there is no delete or empty-value path). So an implementer told to make this refuse cannot construct an input. The reachable instance is `tp import`: internal/cli/importcmd.go:158 carries the existing workflow block forward only when the imported document has NO top-level `workflow` key (importedHasWorkflowKey is a raw-JSON top-level key check); an imported document that DOES carry a workflow block omitting audit_converge_on replaces the block and drops a task-level `all`, uncovering a project-level `blocking`. That write names neither literal, so an implementer following §3's three enumerated shapes (a literal blocking, all-then-blocking, an import carrying blocking forward) ships the hole. §3's table row 1 also misstates import: it carries forward when the DOCUMENT omits the workflow key, not when it omits the field.
suggestion: Replace the impossible example and fix the table row. §3's paragraph should read: "'Resolved' means resolved, not stored at the written layer. A --project write of `blocking` under a task override of `all` changes nothing an audit will read, and must pass. The refusal is not always a write of `blocking`: an import whose workflow block is present but omits the field drops a task-level `all` and uncovers a project-level `blocking`, changing the resolved value without naming either literal, and is refused. The comparison is resolved-before against resolved-after, at every sink, over the whole block a sink writes rather than over the keys it names." §3's table row 1's `fails on` cell should say "...carries the existing block forward only when the imported DOCUMENT omits the top-level workflow key; a present-but-partial block drops the field." Add a §7 row: "| 13b | §3 *the change rule* | an import whose workflow block is present and omits the field, over a task-level `all` and a project-level `blocking`, is refused under TP_UNATTENDED=1 | a fence that compares only the keys the write names |"

finding: §3's canonical illustration of the change rule is impossible under the precedence §2 states, and it contradicts a sentence three lines above it. §3: "a `--project` write of `all` that *uncovers* a task override of `blocking` changes the resolved value and must be refused." Under §2's precedence — task override > project config > built-in, pinned by §7 test 2 and implemented in engine/configresolve.go ResolveWorkflowLayers, which reads the task override first for every field — a task override of `blocking` is never covered by anything: it already wins before the write and still wins after it. Resolved-before equals resolved-after, so by §3's own rule that write must PASS. The project layer is the lower one; a project write cannot uncover a task override, only the reverse (removing a task override of `all` uncovers a project `blocking`, and that is a deletion, not a write of `all`). The paragraph is also falsified in the other direction by §3 line 156-157: "a write of `all` never trips it, since `all` is the default and the only value that tightens the gate". §7 test 13 takes that second side ("the writes that must **pass**: any write of `all`"), so whichever reading is intended, one of §3 and §7 is wrong and an implementer cannot tell which.
suggestion: Delete the uncover clause or restate it in the only direction the precedence admits: a write or removal at the TASK layer that uncovers a project-layer `blocking` changes the resolved value and is refused. Then reconcile 'a write of `all` never trips it' with whichever cases survive, and make §7 test 13 name the surviving set rather than 'any write of `all`'.

finding: §4 asserts '--merge can evaluate that condition -- it holds the round's rows and resolves the same field --record will.' It cannot resolve the same field, and the code says why. internal/cli/audit_merge.go lines 26-37 reject a spec-looking positional at entry with exit 2 ('--merge takes NDJSON input files only'), so tp audit --merge is structurally never told which spec the round belongs to. §2 puts *task override* at the top of the precedence, and that layer lives in <base>.tasks.json keyed by the spec base. Whenever a task override is set, --merge and --record can resolve different values and §4's emission condition then fires on one command and not the other. §7 tests 15, 16 and 17 all assert by_severity without pinning which layer --merge read, so an implementation consulting only the project config passes all three, and so does one consulting the active pointer instead. Wrong if: §4 named the layers --merge reads, or this release gave --merge a way to learn the spec.
suggestion: State the resolution --merge actually performs, in §4: 'Because --merge takes only NDJSON inputs and refuses a spec-looking positional, it resolves audit_converge_on from the project config and the built-in only -- a task override does not reach it. Where the two layers disagree, --merge's breakdown is advisory and --record's verdict governs.' Add row 15c: '| 15c | §4 *resolution* | with a task override of blocking over a project config of all, --merge follows the project layer and --record follows the override, and the spec names which is authoritative | a fixture with no task override, where the two layers cannot disagree |'.

finding: §4 gates emission on a workflow field at a sink that has no spec context and, by shipped design, refuses one — so 'resolves the same field `--record` will' cannot hold. §4: "`--merge` can evaluate that condition — it holds the round's rows and resolves the same field `--record` will." Measured: `engine.ResolveWorkflow(specPath, explicitFile)` (internal/engine/workflow_resolve.go:16-36) reaches the task-override layer only through `specMatches(tfPath, tf.Spec, specPath)` or `SpecAdjacentTaskFile(specPath)`; with no spec path both branches fall through and resolution degrades to project config > built-in, dropping the top layer of the precedence §2 states and §7 test 2 pins. `runAuditMerge` (internal/cli/audit_merge.go:19-46) takes only NDJSON inputs and rejects a spec-looking positional at entry with exit 2, while `--record` resolves against the spec named on ITS command line (audit_record.go:44, :91). The only substitute available to `--merge` is `DiscoverTaskFile(".", flagFile)` — the active pointer — which in a repository with several task files in flight (this one) resolves a DIFFERENT spec's override from the one the round belongs to, so the key would appear or vanish according to `.tp/local.json`, silently; §7 tests 15/16 pin presence without pinning whose policy decided it. REFERENCE.md:762 records that `--merge` carries no policy-aware output today, which is the invariant being changed without saying so.
suggestion: State the resolution rule for `--merge` explicitly: either give it an explicit selector (a spec or `--file`) for the policy it resolves, or specify that it resolves project config > built-in only, say so where §2 states the precedence, and add a §7 row asserting which layer `--merge` reads. Either way drop 'the same field `--record` will' unless a mechanism makes it true.

finding: §4's bucket paragraph specifies a population its own emission predicate makes empty. The key is emitted only when the merged round would be clean under the resolved policy AND holds at least one non-PASS row. Under `all` that is unreachable (§4 says so). Under `blocking` a clean round is one where no non-PASS row carries a blocking severity, and §2 makes `error` and every unrecognised shape blocking - so on every round that emits `by_severity`, the `error` bucket is 0 and the `unrecognised` bucket is 0 by construction. The paragraph spends its whole argument (four unrecognised shapes, the empty-string-is-not-a-bucket rule, `error` + `unrecognised` sums the round's blocking rows so 'the two sections cannot drift apart') on two buckets that can only ever be zero wherever the key exists. The only bytes the key can carry are `warning` and `info`, and the drift-detection property §4 claims is unbuyable at this emission point.
suggestion: Emit `by_severity` unconditionally over the round's non-PASS rows. That is the only emission point at which `error` and `unrecognised` can be non-zero, and the only one at which the sum property detects drift against §2. If the predicate is kept, delete the four-shape/empty-string/sum paragraph and say plainly that the key carries the advisory mix only.

finding: §4's emission condition and §2's blocking set exclude each other, so two of §4's paragraphs and one test row specify a population that can never be observed. §4 emits by_severity 'when the merged round would be clean under the resolved policy AND holds at least one non-PASS row'. §2 defines clean under blocking as 'no non-PASS row in the round carries a blocking severity', and the blocking severities are error plus every unrecognised shape. Therefore in EVERY round where by_severity is emitted, the error bucket and the unrecognised bucket are necessarily 0. §4's stated invariant -- 'error + unrecognised sums the round's blocking rows and the two sections cannot drift apart' -- is always 0 = 0 on the only surface it is stated for. §7 test 17 is not merely weak, it is unwritable: its fixture 'carrying all four unrecognised shapes' is by construction a round that does not emit the key, and both wrong implementations it names (an empty-string bucket, splitting the four) also pass, because the buckets they corrupt are empty. §4 closes the second branch itself: 'Under all the condition is unreachable by construction'. Wrong if: §4 emitted by_severity on every merged round holding a non-PASS row, or §2's blocking set excluded unrecognised -- either makes the buckets reachable.
suggestion: Decide which surface carries the buckets and say so; do not keep both. (a) Replace §4's emission condition with 'Emitted on every merged round that holds at least one non-PASS row, and it survives --compact', delete the paragraph justifying the clean half, and test 17 becomes writable as written. Or (b) keep the clean-gated emission, delete the error/unrecognised buckets and test 17, and replace the invariant sentence with: 'On an emitted round every bucket is advisory by construction -- an error row or an unrecognised one would have made the round unclean, so the key never has to distinguish them.'

finding: §4's emission condition and §4's bucket invariant are mutually exclusive, so the invariant can never be observed on an emitted key and §7 test 17 has no constructible fixture. The condition: by_severity is emitted only when "the merged round would be clean under the resolved policy AND holds at least one non-PASS row". The invariant: "error + unrecognised sums the round's blocking rows". §2 makes unrecognised blocking ("An unrecognised severity is treated as blocking") and error blocking ("Blocking severity is error"). A round clean under blocking therefore has zero blocking rows by definition, so on every round where by_severity is emitted, error + unrecognised is identically 0 and the sum carries no information. Test 17 asks for the assertion "over a fixture carrying all four unrecognised shapes" -- four blocking rows -- which is exactly a round that is NOT clean under blocking, so by_severity is absent and the test cannot read the buckets it asserts over. An implementer must invent one of: emit on unclean rounds too, exempt unrecognised from blocking, or drop the sum. Falsifier checked: §4 would have to state a second emission case, or §2 would have to grade unrecognised as non-blocking. §4 line 183-184 states one condition only; §2 line 64-66 states the fail-closed rule normatively.
suggestion: Split the two claims and state both. Replace the closing clause of §4's bucket paragraph with: "error + unrecognised is the round's blocking-row count, which is 0 on every round that carries the key -- the invariant is what makes that zero readable rather than a coincidence of one implementation. It is asserted on the counter itself, not on an emitted payload." And rewrite §7 row 17 to: "| 17 | §4 *buckets* | the by_severity counter over a round carrying all four unrecognised shapes puts every one in `unrecognised`, so error + unrecognised equals that round's blocking-row count -- asserted on the counter directly, since such a round is not clean under blocking and so carries no emitted key | a \"\" bucket, or splitting the four |"

finding: §4's emission predicate, added this round, makes the two buckets §4 exists to protect identically zero on every payload that carries the key. Emission: "when the merged round would be clean under the resolved policy *and* holds at least one non-`PASS` row". Buckets: "`error` + `unrecognised` sums the round's blocking rows and the two sections cannot drift apart." By §2's predicate a round is clean under `blocking` exactly when no non-`PASS` row carries a blocking severity, and §2 makes an unrecognised severity blocking — so on every emitted `by_severity`, `error` = 0 and `unrecognised` = 0 by construction; under `all` the key is never emitted at all. The sum §4 names is therefore always 0 = 0. Consequences: (a) 'Every row lands in a named bucket, because the point is that nothing hides' is true only of `warning` and `info`, the two that never hid; (b) '`""` is not a bucket … it is the hiding this section exists to prevent' guards a population that cannot appear; (c) §7 test 17 ('`error` + `unrecognised` equals the round's blocking-row count over a fixture carrying all four unrecognised shapes') cannot be written against an emitted payload, and its named killing input — 'a `""` bucket, or splitting the four' — does not kill, because every bucketing rule agrees on an empty population.
suggestion: Decide which §4 wants. Either emit `by_severity` on every round holding a non-`PASS` row (so `error`/`unrecognised` are reachable and the sum is checkable, at the cost of the presence signal §4 argues for), or keep the clean-only condition and drop the `error`/`unrecognised` reachability argument and test 17 with it, stating instead that an emitted breakdown holds only advisory severities by construction.

finding: Test 17 is unwritable against §4 as written, and rows 15 and 17 cannot both pass. Row 17 asserts `error` + `unrecognised` equals the round's blocking-row count over a fixture carrying all four unrecognised shapes. A fixture carrying unrecognised shapes carries blocking rows (§2 fail-closed), so that round is not clean under `blocking`, so row 15's assertion (`by_severity` present only on a round clean-under-blocking holding non-PASS rows, absent otherwise) requires the key to be absent - there is nothing for row 17 to sum. The derivation column is what should have caught this: rows 15 and 17 both cite §4 and derive contradictory observables from it, which is the same one-round lag §7's preamble says the column exists to make visible.
suggestion: Resolve §4 first - unconditional emission makes both rows writable as stated. If the predicate stands, restate row 17 as an assertion over `--record`'s blocking count rather than over a `by_severity` map that cannot exist on such a round.

finding: §7 test 13 and §3 give opposite answers about the same write. Test 13: the writes that must pass are 'any write of all, and an import carrying an already-resolved blocking forward'. §3, four paragraphs earlier: 'a --project write of all that *uncovers* a task override of blocking changes the resolved value and must be refused.' An engineer writing test 13 from the row ships a fence that lets the uncovering write through; one writing it from §3 ships a test the row calls a failure. Neither of §3's two worked cases -- the --project write of blocking under a task override of all that must PASS, and the --project write of all that uncovers blocking and must be REFUSED -- appears in test 12 or 13. So §3's longest normative passage, the one defining the comparison as resolved-before against resolved-after at every sink, has no row deriving from it. Wrong if: §3's 'Resolved means resolved' paragraph did not exist, or test 13 read 'any write of all that does not uncover a higher-layer blocking'.
suggestion: Rewrite test 13's assertion as: 'the writes that must **pass**: a write of all that leaves the resolved value all; a --project write of blocking under a task override of all, which changes nothing an audit reads; and an import carrying an already-resolved blocking forward -- three assertions'. Then add row 13b: '| 13b | §3 *resolved not stored* | a --project write of all that uncovers a task override of blocking is refused, because the resolved value changes to blocking | a fence comparing the written literal instead of resolved-before against resolved-after |'.

finding: §2 decides what `clean` means under `blocking` and leaves `findings` -- the field `clean` is computed from today and the field §7 test 10 needs -- undecided, so two observably different implementations both satisfy the spec. In the tree `clean := findings == 0` (internal/cli/audit_record.go:71) and `findings` is both an emitted top-level key (line 99) and a stored round field (`engine.ReviewRound.Findings`, recordAuditRoundEntry line 207). Under `blocking` the two must separate, and §2 never says which way: either `findings` keeps counting every non-PASS row and `clean` is computed beside it, or `findings` becomes policy-aware and reports 0 on an accepted-open round. §2's boundary paragraph names exactly three fields that stay severity-blind -- `role_streaks[].open`, its `consecutive_clean`, and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` -- and §7's closing "Not tested here, named so the absence is deliberate" paragraph repeats the same three. `findings` is in neither list. It is not a cosmetic choice: §2 requires `next_action` to name "how many non-PASS rows were accepted" and §7 test 10 pins that number, and on the `--status` path (audit_record.go:390) the only source for it is the latest stored round's `Findings` -- which is zero under the second reading, leaving test 10 unimplementable there.
suggestion: Decide it in §2, in the boundary paragraph. Change "`role_streaks[].open`, its `consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` stay severity-blind" to "`findings` -- both the emitted key and the value stored on the round -- keeps counting every non-`PASS` row under both values, so `clean` and `findings` separate under `blocking` and the accepted count `next_action` names is readable from a stored round without re-reading its rows. `role_streaks[].open`, its `consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` stay severity-blind for the same reason." Then add the same field to §7's closing paragraph or give it a row: "| 10b | §2 *next_action* | a round recorded clean under `blocking` still stores and emits `findings` equal to its non-`PASS` row count, which is where `--status` reads the accepted count | making `findings` policy-aware, which zeroes the number test 10 asserts |"

finding: The release computes exactly the number the knob's decision needs and then hides it on every round where the decision is made. §2.1 establishes that the field must resolve before round 1 is recorded, so the operator decides on the *previous* cycle's severity mix - and §4's predicate emits `by_severity` only on a round already clean under `blocking`. A cycle running under the default `all` (the case §2.1 is written for) never produces a single `by_severity`, because under `all` the condition is unreachable by construction. So the previous cycle leaves no breakdown anywhere, and §2.1's answer is that the operator hand-counts `severity` across `audit-round-*.ndjson` with a shell recipe carried in SKILL.md. The release therefore ships a counter, suppresses it precisely where its output is decision-bearing, and replaces it with a manual round-trip over 22 files - the opposite of the AX trade the field is sold on.
suggestion: Make the breakdown available where the decision is made: emit `by_severity` unconditionally on `--merge` (see §4). The recipe then documents a fallback for cycles recorded before the release rather than being the only path; §2.1's 'the release owes the operator that number at the moment they need it' becomes true rather than aspirational.

finding: The change rule closes the two deadlocks the table names and leaves a third one reachable, through the very configuration §3 declares legal. §3 says a `--project` write of `blocking` under a task override of `all` "changes nothing an audit will read, and must pass" — so a project may legitimately end up with project `blocking` under task `all`. Now run Workflow A step 6 in that project. `tp import` carries the existing workflow block forward only when the imported document has NO top-level workflow key (internal/cli/importcmd.go:158 `!importedHasWorkflowKey(trimmed)`); a decomposer's tasks.json that carries `"workflow": {}` — the exact shape this repository's own v0.26.0 migration wrote into its task files — skips preservation, so `tf.Workflow` becomes empty, the task-level `all` is dropped, and the project's `blocking` becomes the resolved value. resolved-before `all`, resolved-after `blocking`: the change rule refuses it. The import never mentions `audit_converge_on`, the unit cannot make it pass by editing the document (adding the field back is itself a write the fence must judge), and Workflow A step 6 deadlocks under `tp run` for an opt-in project — the same failure round 9 reported against the value-scoped fence, arriving by a different route the new table does not list.
suggestion: Add a fourth row to §3's table for it, and decide the case: either an import that changes the resolved value only by dropping a shadowing layer is exempt (the project layer was operator-approved, so nothing new is being approved by a unit), or `tp import` must preserve a task-level `audit_converge_on` across a workflow-block replacement the way it preserves the whole block today. Whichever is chosen, §7 needs the row, since row 13's "an import carrying an already-resolved `blocking` forward" does not cover an import that changes the resolved value to `blocking` by removing an override.

finding: Round 10 tightened §4's emission condition and stranded the paragraph and the test that depend on the old one. Round 9's snapshot (spec/.tp-review/0.37.0/snapshot-round-9.md:165) reads "Emitted when the round has at least one non-`PASS` row"; round 10 reads "Emitted when the merged round would be clean under the resolved policy *and* holds at least one non-`PASS` row". Under §2 a round is clean under `blocking` only when no non-`PASS` row carries a blocking severity, and an unrecognised severity IS blocking. So on every round where `by_severity` is emitted, `error` == 0 and `unrecognised` == 0 by construction; under `all` the key never appears at all. That makes §4's own claim — "`error` + `unrecognised` sums the round's blocking rows and the two sections cannot drift apart" — the identity 0 == 0, which can detect no drift, and it makes §7 row 17 unwritable: its fixture "carrying all four unrecognised shapes" is by definition not clean under `blocking`, so `by_severity` is absent and there are no buckets to sum. Only `warning` and `info` can ever be non-zero in an emitted breakdown. This is the failure §7's preamble says round 9 measured — "four tests demanding the implementation the sections had just rejected" — reappearing on the round the derivation column was added to prevent it.
suggestion: Pick one. Either keep the clean-gated emission and cut the blocking-row-sum claim and row 17 — the emitted breakdown is a warning/info breakdown and saying so is honest — or state that `by_severity` is also emitted on an unclean round so the invariant has a population, which reopens the "key on every round that has any finding" case round 10 just closed. Either way row 17's falsifying input must name a fixture the emission condition can reach.

finding: The conditional emission buys at most four integers and pays for them with a new dependency for `tp audit --merge`, plus a preview that can disagree with the sink it previews. §4 asserts '`--merge` can evaluate that condition - it holds the round's rows and resolves the same field `--record` will.' It holds the rows; it does not hold the second half. `--merge` takes NDJSON inputs only and rejects a spec-looking positional at entry, so it has no spec and no task file: to resolve a *task override* it must acquire discovery plus the active pointer, gaining a config-read path, a resolution-failure mode outside a tp project, and a coupling that `by_status`/`by_role`/`findings` - the counters it sits beside in the same loop - do not have. And the resolution it performs is not necessarily the one `--record <spec>` performs seconds later, because in a multi-spec repo (tp's own has many `spec/*.tasks.json`) the discovered task file need not be the one that spec's `--record` reads. The key can then be present on a round `--record` grades unclean, or absent on one it grades clean - the exact preview error the deliverable exists to prevent.
suggestion: Emit `by_severity` unconditionally over the round's non-PASS rows, beside `by_status` and `by_role`, and let the policy live only where it is already resolved (`--record`). It costs at most four integers on rounds that have findings and nothing on an all-PASS round; it removes the config dependency, the divergence, tests 15's absence half and 17's contradiction; and it is the shape that lets §2.1's operator read the previous cycle's mix at all (see the §2.1 finding).

finding: §4 asserts "`--merge` can evaluate that condition -- it holds the round's rows and resolves the same field `--record` will", and that is not buildable: `--merge` has no spec argument, and `--record`'s resolution is keyed on one. Measured in the tree: `runAuditMerge(args []string, outputPath string)` (internal/cli/audit_merge.go:19) takes only NDJSON paths and rejects a spec-looking positional at entry with exit 2 (lines 29-38); `runAuditRecord` resolves with `engine.ResolveWorkflow(specPath, flagFile)` (audit_record.go:44,91), and `ResolveWorkflow` (internal/engine/workflow_resolve.go:16-36) uses the spec THREE times -- it accepts the discovered task file only when `specMatches(tfPath, tf.Spec, specPath)`, then falls back to `SpecAdjacentTaskFile(specPath)`, then to project-only. So `--merge`, which can only reach `DiscoverTaskFile(".", flagFile)`, resolves a different layer stack from `--record` exactly when the active task file's `spec` field is not the spec being audited -- which is the normal state in this repository, where fourteen `spec/*.tasks.json` files sit beside one `.tp/local.json` active pointer. The result is a key that appears or disappears on `--merge` disagreeing with the `clean` `--record` stamps one command later, which is the opposite of the readability §1 deliverable 3 promises.
suggestion: State the input. Add to §4, after "`--merge` can evaluate that condition": "It resolves the field from the same two layers `--record` does, but without a spec it cannot use `ResolveWorkflow`'s spec-matching path. `--merge` therefore takes the spec it is merging for: `tp audit <spec> --merge <a.ndjson> ...` -- the positional §4.1 currently refuses -- OR the release states that `--merge` resolves through the discovered task file and its project config alone, and §7 gains a row pinning the case where the two disagree." Whichever is chosen, add a §7 row: "| 15b | §4 | `--merge` and the `--record` that follows it resolve the same value when the active task file's `spec` field names a different spec | resolving `--merge` through task-file discovery while `--record` resolves through the spec |"

finding: §6a closes the reversal set at three ("The count is three because earlier drafts said one and then two"), and at least two further shipped assertions are falsified by §2 — both in the same document §6a already edits. (1) `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:753-756`: "The audit gate is untouched: `engine.Converged`, `engine.ConsecutiveClean`, the stored per-round `clean` flag, the exit code of `tp audit --status --check`, and `next_action`'s three-state audit precedence all behave exactly as in v0.32.0." §2 changes the stored `clean` flag's meaning, changes which `next_action` branch fires and adds a fourth recommendation, and therefore changes `--status --check`'s exit code on the same rounds. (2) `internal/engine/nextaction.go:63-75` documents the same 'three-state precedence' in the constructor's own doc comment, so the count §2 makes four is pinned in code as well as docs. §6a's closing claim — "Each replacement states a rule true under **both** values of the field" — cannot be satisfied for artifacts the section does not name, and §6a's own reason for existing (a decomposer reads this list to size the coordinated edit) is what the omission defeats.
suggestion: Re-derive the reversal set by searching the shipped artifacts for assertions over `clean`, `next_action`'s branch count and `--status --check`, and state the count as whatever that search returns rather than as a corrected literal. At minimum add REFERENCE.md:753-756 and nextaction.go's 'three-state precedence' comment, and extend §7 test 19 to cover them.

finding: §6a requires three coordinated edits and never states the replacement text, and §7 test 19 inherits the gap: 'SKILL.md and REFERENCE.md both state a rule true under **both** values'. 'States a rule true under both values' is not a pass/fail predicate -- no assertion can evaluate the truth of an arbitrary English sentence under two configurations. Two engineers write contradictory tests from that row: one asserts the ABSENCE of the old sentence, one asserts a SPECIFIC new sentence they invented, and both claim the row implemented. The guard the row names asserts literals (§6a itself says so: 'once as a test-local literal against SKILL.md's own prose, and once as engine.DivergenceHint against REFERENCE.md'), so the release cannot be built without the literal, and the spec is the only place it can be decided once for three artifacts that §6a says must move together. Wrong if: §6a gave the replacement sentence.
suggestion: State the sentence in §6a and have test 19 assert it verbatim. E.g.: 'The replacement, used verbatim in all three places: "Audit convergence counts every non-PASS row whose severity blocks under the resolved audit_converge_on; under the default all, that is every non-PASS row."' Then test 19 reads: 'SKILL.md, REFERENCE.md and engine.DivergenceHint all carry §6a's replacement sentence verbatim, asserted twice and independently by the docs-contract guard | editing the constant alone, which leaves SKILL.md green and false'.

finding: §7 test 18 asserts 'all **nine** surviving assertions of the gate guard still pass' and §6a item 1 says 'Two of its eleven assertions; the other nine stand'. The spec names neither the file, the test function, nor the counting rule, so the number is unreproducible from the spec. Counted here: TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate in internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go lines 469-503 holds 11 assert./require. call sites -- lines 473, 474, 481, 484, 485, 490, 493, 494, 497, 498, 500, from a regex faster_search for '(assert|require)' followed by a dot over that file, restricted to lines >= 469 -- two of which are the reversed pair, so nine survive under the rule 'one assertion = one assert/require call site'. Under an equally natural rule the number moves: excluding the two require.True(t, ok) decode-plumbing checks gives 9 and 7, and counting distinct claims rather than call sites gives fewer again. Separately the row is not discriminating: 'the nine still pass' is satisfied by any tree in which that file compiles green, so its named failing input ('keeping two and deleting seven') does NOT fail it -- deleting assertions makes a count wrong and the row asserts no count. Wrong if: §6a named the file and function and defined the counting rule, and test 18 asserted the count rather than the passing.
suggestion: In §6a item 1 write: 'The gate guard is TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate in internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go. Counting one assert./require. call site as one assertion, it holds eleven; the two at the top -- that tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking exits non-zero, and that stdout+stderr contains "unknown workflow field: audit_converge_on" -- are reversed, and the other nine stand.' Then test 18 becomes: 'the gate guard still holds exactly eleven assert/require call sites, the two named ones now assert acceptance, and the file is green | deleting the seven that are inconvenient, which leaves a green file'.

finding: §2 says 'Both audit sinks compute next_action from the round's clean' and that the new branch 'names how many non-PASS rows were accepted'. §7 test 10 asserts one recommendation, names no sink, and pins the count only as 'names how many'. Test 12 shows §7 knows how to close this ('three assertions, one per path'); test 10 does not, so an implementation that changes the branch on --record and leaves --status on the old text passes it. And 'names how many' is not a form: '3 findings accepted' and 'three findings accepted' both satisfy it, so two engineers write assertions that disagree on whether a decimal numeral is required -- and a substring check for the count is what the test must do, since the row's own falsifying input is a text difference. Wrong if: §2 said which sink carries the sentence, or test 10 said 'on both --record and --status' and named the form.
suggestion: Rewrite test 10: 'under blocking, a clean round holding k non-PASS rows produces a recommendation on **both** --record and --status containing the decimal numeral k, textually different from the one an empty round produces -- two assertions, one per sink | deriving the branch from clean alone, or changing one sink and leaving the other'. Add one sentence to §2's next_action paragraph: 'The count appears as a decimal numeral, so a test can assert it as a substring.'

finding: §7 test 15's absent case is 'an all-PASS round', which does not discriminate the implementation §4 explicitly rejects. §4 says an earlier draft 'took the count half and dropped the clean half, which puts the key on every round that has any finding'. A count-only implementation emits nothing on an all-PASS round too, because the count is zero -- so test 15 passes under the very draft §4 spends a paragraph rejecting, and its named failing input ('emitting unconditionally') is a strictly weaker mutant that the count-only draft is not. The two cases that separate the drafts are absent from §7 entirely: a round NOT clean under blocking that holds non-PASS rows, and any round under audit_converge_on: all that holds non-PASS rows. Wrong if: test 15's absent case named an unclean round holding findings rather than an all-PASS round.
suggestion: Split test 15 into two rows: '| 15 | §4 | by_severity is present on a round clean under blocking that holds non-PASS rows | emitting unconditionally |' and '| 15b | §4 *the clean half* | **absent** on a round holding error rows under blocking, and absent on a round holding non-PASS rows under all -- the two cases an all-PASS round cannot separate | the count-only draft §4 rejects, which passes an all-PASS absent case |'.

finding: §7 test 9 asserts that switching to blocking 'leaves every stored round's **reported** verdict unchanged -- reported, not stored'. There is no emitted form of 'every stored round's verdict'. tp audit --status/--record report clean for the LATEST round only (internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go reads out[round], out[clean], out[consecutive_clean] off one payload); the only surface carrying every round's verdict is state.json, which the row forbids by name. So the row is writable only as a one-round assertion, and the multi-round property §2 actually decides -- that engine.ConsecutiveClean over the stored rounds does not move when the knob flips -- is asserted by nothing in §7. The row's justification is separately unverifiable from the spec: §2 says 'the review twin recomputes live', the row says 'the twin stamps too'. Both are true of the code (internal/engine/reviewstate.go:20 stores 'Clean bool'; internal/cli/review_record.go:194 reports a recomputed liveClean), but §2 states only half, so a reader of §2 alone concludes the row's premise is false and writes the stored-bytes assertion the row forbids. Wrong if: the row named an emitted per-round list, or asserted consecutive_clean and converged rather than a per-round verdict.
suggestion: Make the observable the aggregate, which is emitted. Rewrite test 9: 'recording n rounds under all and then setting blocking without re-recording leaves clean, consecutive_clean and converged on --status byte-identical to their values before the switch | a live re-grade at read time'. And complete §2's stamping paragraph: 'The review twin does both -- it stores a clean flag on the round and reports a recomputed one. Only the reported value separates the two designs, which is why the audit side is specified on what it reports.'

finding: §7 was rewritten this round as a derivation table whose stated purpose is that "a decision that changes and leaves its row untouched is visible", and it already fails on §3's newest decision. §3's paragraph "**\"Resolved\" means resolved, not stored at the written layer**" carries two normative cases — a `--project` write of `blocking` under a task override of `all` must PASS, and a write that uncovers a task-level `blocking` must be REFUSED — and neither has a row. Row 12 derives from "§3 *the change rule*" and covers only refusals of a write of `blocking`; row 13 derives from the same and lists "any write of `all`" and "an import carrying an already-resolved `blocking` forward" as the passes. The one case that discriminates a resolved-scoped fence from a fence scoped to the written layer — writing `blocking` at the project layer under a task `all` — appears in no row, so an implementation comparing the value written at its own layer instead of the resolved value passes all nineteen rows. The column introduced to make an unmaintained row visible did not make this one visible on the round it was introduced.
suggestion: Add a row deriving from "§3 *resolved, not stored*": a `--project` write of `blocking` under a task override of `all` exits 0 under TP_UNATTENDED=1, falsifying input "a fence comparing the value written at its own layer rather than the resolved value". Add the mirror refusal row once §3's uncover case is restated on a reachable sink, and drop or qualify "any write of `all`" in row 13 so it does not contradict that paragraph.

finding: §7's premise is "Every test here is derived from a numbered decision above, and the derivation is written down", and row 4 has no such decision. Row 4 cites "§2 *The field*" and asserts "`tp config --extract` emits the field; `tp validate --project` accepts a legal value and rejects an illegal one". §2 *The field* (lines 42-45) says only: the value set, the resolution precedence, and refusal at the write and consuming sinks. Neither `tp config --extract` nor `tp validate --project` appears anywhere in §2, §2.1, §3, §4 or §6a -- the row's stated justification is a history note ("v0.31.0 shipped the twin without both and needed v0.31.1"), not a decision this spec makes. This is the failure the derivation column exists to expose, in the direction the column cannot catch: the column is checked by reading down from §7, and a row citing a real anchor that does not carry the claim reads as covered. It matters for building because the two commands are real work -- internal/cli/config_extract.go's `computeCommonPolicy`, `hoistedFields` and `mergeCommon` each need a new line, and internal/cli/validate_project.go needs a deviation branch -- and nothing normative in the spec asks for any of it.
suggestion: Give the row a decision to derive from. Add to §2 *The field*, after the sink sentence: "The field is a project-config field like its twin, so it is hoisted by `tp config --extract` and reported by `tp validate --project` when a task override deviates from the project value. v0.31.0 shipped `review_converge_on` without both and needed v0.31.1 to add them; this release ships them together." Then row 4's `derives from` cell reads "§2 *The field*" truthfully.

finding: §1 deliverable 3's replacement text is still the inverse of §4's rule, in a new way. §1: "the breakdown that makes a `blocking` round's verdict readable, emitted on the rounds where there is something to read." §4 emits it only when the round would be CLEAN under the resolved policy and holds a non-`PASS` row — so it is absent on every round whose verdict is 'not clean', which is the round where an operator asks what blocked it and the only round on which `error` and `unrecognised` are non-zero. The rounds where there is most to read are exactly the rounds with no breakdown. §1 also still presents deliverable 3 as one of three things the release buys while, by §4's own paragraph, the key is unreachable by construction for every project on the default — which §1 deliverable 1 says is every project that does not set the field.
suggestion: Restate deliverable 3 as what §4 decides: the breakdown that shows what a clean-under-`blocking` round accepted, emitted only on such a round and therefore only for projects that opt in. Do not paraphrase §4's condition in §1 at all if the two keep diverging — name the section and stop.

finding: Two normative clauses of this release have no row deriving from them, in a §7 whose opening sentence is 'Every test here is derived from a numbered decision above'. (a) §2: invalid values are refused 'on the same terms and with the same hint as review_converge_on'. Test 3 asserts the two error KINDS -- usage error at the write sink, validation error at the consuming sink -- and says nothing about the hint, so hint parity ships unasserted. That is the exact class of config/doc parity that cost this project v0.31.1, which test 4's own cell cites as the reason test 4 exists. (b) §2.1: 'skills/tp/SKILL.md carries the one-line command that derives it, next to the field's documentation.' That is a deliverable of this release, the spec never states the command, and no row derives from it -- while the docs-contract guard §6a already reaches SKILL.md, so it is the cheapest assertion in the release and is currently asserted nowhere. Wrong if: test 3 named the hint, and §2.1 stated the command.
suggestion: Extend test 3: '... a validation error -- and both messages carry the same hint text review_converge_on's sinks emit, with this field's name substituted | asserting the exit codes only'. State the command in §2.1 as a literal, then add row 4b: '| 4b | §2.1 *the number the operator needs* | skills/tp/SKILL.md carries §2.1's derivation command verbatim, beside the field's documentation, asserted by the docs-contract guard | documenting the field without the command, which leaves the operator no basis for the decision |'.

finding: §2 justifies a bespoke `next_action` string with a claim §4 refutes four paragraphs later. §2: the branch 'is the only place an operator learns that a round closed over open rows: it states that the phase may proceed and names how many non-PASS rows were accepted'. §4: 'The *count* of them is already emitted - `role_streaks[].open` is severity-blind and unconditional on both `--status` and `--record` - so what is missing is the **breakdown**'. Both statements are about the same `--record` payload. The count `next_action` renders into prose is therefore a sum over an array already in the same response, and 'the only place' is false. The cost is not the integer: it is a hand-written sentence, a decision §2 says it makes 'rather than leaving it to an implementer', and test row 10 pinning a textual difference - all to re-say a number the payload carries structurally.
suggestion: Keep the branch (a clean-with-open-rows round must not read like an empty one) and drop the restated count: let `next_action` name the action and the fact of acceptance, and let `role_streaks[].open` carry the number. Row 10 then asserts the branch difference, which is the property that matters, without pinning a rendered count that can drift from the array beside it.

finding: §2's `next_action` decision, strengthened this round, ships the information §6 Non-Goal 4 defers, on the surface Non-Goal 4 defers it from. §2 now requires that under `blocking` the recommendation "states that the phase may proceed and names how many non-`PASS` rows were accepted", and `next_action` is emitted by both audit sinks — internal/cli/audit_record.go:125 (`--record`) and :391 (`--status`). §6 Non-Goal 4 defers "`nonblocking_open` on `--record` and `--status`" because "four places pin its absence there by name". The four guards pin a key, so nothing reddens; but the accepted-open count is now delivered on `--record` and `--status` regardless, as a substring instead of a field. The deferral therefore defers the shape and not the information, and an agent parsing the count out of prose is worse off than one reading a key — which is the AX argument the deferral was resting on.
suggestion: Say so in Non-Goal 4: what is deferred is the `nonblocking_open` key, not the fact, because §2 puts the count in `next_action`'s text on the same two commands. If that reads as an admission the key should just ship, that is the honest reading and belongs in §6 rather than being left for a decomposer to notice.

finding: The SKILL.md recipe is a deliverable nothing in this release verifies. §2.1 makes it the operator's only route to the decision input ('No flag is added for this. `skills/tp/SKILL.md` carries the one-line command that derives it'), yet §1 lists three deliverables and the recipe is in none of them, and §7's twenty rows cover no assertion over it - while row 19 does pin SKILL.md's *other* sentence through the docs-contract guard. A shell one-liner over NDJSON that no test runs is exactly the artifact this repo has already been burned by: an under-specified recipe returns a plausible wrong answer and nothing reddens.
suggestion: Either name it in §1 as part of deliverable 1's documentation and give §7 a row that runs it against a committed round file and compares its output to the expected mix, or remove the reliance on it by emitting `by_severity` unconditionally (§4 finding), leaving the recipe as convenience prose rather than the decision's only basis.

finding: §2.1 places a normative documentation obligation on the release -- "`skills/tp/SKILL.md` carries the one-line command that derives it, next to the field's documentation, so the decision has a stated basis rather than a suggestion to go and look" -- and no §7 row derives from it, while §7's closing paragraph ("Not tested here, named so the absence is deliberate") lists only `role_streaks[].open`, its `consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`. So the clause is neither tested nor declared deliberately untested, which is exactly the hole the derivation column was added to expose. It is testable the way the release already tests documents: internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go asserts pinned substrings over `readRepoDoc(t, "skills/tp/SKILL.md")` today (lines 131-135), and §7 row 19 already reaches SKILL.md for §6a. It is also the clause most likely to be dropped, because it is the only deliverable in the release with no Go code behind it.
suggestion: Add a §7 row: "| 4b | §2.1 *the release owes the operator that number* | `skills/tp/SKILL.md` documents the field and, beside it, the one-line command that counts `severity` across a cycle's `audit-round-*.ndjson` -- asserted as a pinned substring through the docs-contract guard | documenting the field with no way to get the number the decision is made on |" -- or, if it is deliberately untested, name it in §7's closing "Not tested here" paragraph so the absence is a decision rather than an omission.

finding: §2.1's convergence bound is off by one and is falsifiable as stated. "setting it at round *k* converges no earlier than *k* + `audit_clean_rounds`". `engine.Converged` is `ConsecutiveClean(rounds) >= requiredCleanRounds && !stale` and `ConsecutiveClean` is the trailing run (reviewstate.go:428-438, :509-511), so if the field resolves before round *k* is recorded and rounds *k* … *k*+cr−1 are all clean, the streak reaches cr at round *k* + cr − 1 — one round earlier than the stated floor. The table's own k=1, cr=2 cell reads 3 only because v0.35.0's round 1 was not clean under `blocking`; the bound is not tight, and a bound stated as 'no earlier than' is false when a reachable case beats it. The second paragraph's k=1, cr=1 pair (converges at 2) has the same shape.
suggestion: Either write the bound as *k* + `audit_clean_rounds` − 1, or say explicitly that *k* names the last round recorded BEFORE the knob resolves (which makes the stated formula exact) — the surrounding sentence, 'a round recorded before the knob is set keeps `clean: false` for ever', reads the other way.

finding: "The comparison is resolved-before against resolved-after, at every sink" does not say which task file the import sink resolves against, and the one reusable helper resolves the wrong one. `tp import` writes `targetPath`, derived from `tf.Spec` (internal/cli/importcmd.go:141-143), while the existing fence's resolver, `resolvedWorkflowForFence` (internal/cli/unattended.go:90-98), reads `engine.DiscoverTaskFile(".", flagFile)` — the active task file recorded in `.tp/local.json`. In this repository those routinely differ: `tp use` points `active` at the cycle in flight while a new spec's tasks are imported to a different `<base>.tasks.json`. A fence copying the existing helper would compare the resolved value of a task file the import is not writing, and would both refuse legal imports and pass the refusable one. The `tp set --workflow` sink has the mirror of the same gap: it calls `fenceWorkflowWrite` during argument parsing, before `engine.WithFileLock(taskFilePath, ...)` at line 445, so resolved-before is read outside the lock that guards the write.
suggestion: State at §3 that each sink resolves against the file it is about to write — `targetPath` for `tp import`, the discovered task file for `tp set --workflow`, the project config plus that file for the `--project` form — and that the import comparison is made inside the write lock, after the §9.3 workflow-preservation step has decided what `tf.Workflow` will be. Give §7 row 12's import assertion a fixture where the active task file and the import target differ, or the assertion passes on a fence reading either one.

finding: §3 closes an enumeration -- "The three write paths are `tp set --workflow`, its `--project` form, and `tp import`" -- and there is a fourth command that writes both workflow layers. I counted the writers with faster_search over internal/cli: `engine.WriteProjectConfig` has exactly two call sites, set_project.go:195 and config_extract.go:298, and `engine.StripTaskWorkflowFields` has one, config_extract.go:304. So `tp config --extract` writes the project block AND removes the field from every task file, and it already handles the twin (`computeCommonPolicy` line 71, `hoistedFields` line 131, `mergeCommon` line 182). It is resolution-preserving in the case it fires -- `commonPtr` hoists only a value every task file sets identically -- but that is a fact an implementer has to derive, and §3's fence is defined on resolved-before vs resolved-after "at every sink", so a reader has to decide whether `runConfigExtract` is a sink that needs the comparison wired in. Nothing in `runConfigExtract` reads TP_UNATTENDED today.
suggestion: Say four and say why the fourth needs nothing: "The write paths are `tp set --workflow`, its `--project` form, `tp import`, and `tp config --extract`. The first three are fenced. `--extract` hoists only a value every task file already sets identically and strips it from those files in the same write, so resolved-before equals resolved-after by construction and it carries no fence -- stated here so the absence is a decision rather than an oversight." Add a §7 row asserting it: "| 12b | §3 *the change rule* | `tp config --extract` hoisting a unanimous `blocking` leaves the resolved value unchanged and is not refused under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` | fencing every writer of the field rather than every write that changes what resolves |"

finding: §4's bucket rule reverses round 9's decision in the direction the section says it exists to prevent. Round 9 (snapshot-round-9.md:171-176): "A severity that is a string outside the enum keys on that string. A severity that is JSON `null`, absent, or not a string at all keys on **`unrecognised`**" — an unknown string stayed visible. Round 10 folds all four shapes into `unrecognised`, justified by the sum invariant that finding 3 above shows is vacuous under the new emission condition. The cost is the one diagnostic the breakdown could have carried: a typo'd or mis-cased severity (`Error`, `blocker`, `errror`) is exactly the row an operator on `blocking` must find and fix, because §2's fail-closed rule silently makes it blocking, and after round 10 the breakdown no longer names it. "The point is that nothing hides" is now false for the shape most likely to occur, and the reason given for hiding it no longer holds.
suggestion: Restore round 9's split — enum severities and any other string key on themselves, `null`/absent/non-string on `unrecognised` — and if the sum invariant is kept, phrase it as "`error` plus every non-enum bucket" rather than as a two-term sum. That keeps §2's fail-closed population summable without erasing which literal produced it.

finding: The derivation column added this round — §7's stated fix for a test list that lags its decisions — mis-cites in its own first use, and its framing sentence names a structure the spec does not have. Test 8's 'derives from' cell reads '§2 *unrecognised*' and its assertion enumerates four shapes: "outside the enum, `null`, absent, **or not a string** — four fixtures". §2's `unrecognised` paragraph names no shapes at all ("An unrecognised severity is treated as blocking. Not rejected, not ignored. A row tp cannot grade is a row tp must not stop counting."); the four-shape enumeration exists only in §4 ("a string outside the enum, JSON `null`, an absent key, a value that is not a string"). So the row that most needs the column points at a section that cannot move when the enumeration moves — the exact drift the column was introduced to make visible. Separately, §7's opening asserts "Every test here is derived from a **numbered** decision above", while every cell cites an italicised paragraph lead-in (§2 *Default*, §2 *The field*, §2 *stamped*, §4 *buckets*); §2's decisions carry no numbers, so 'numbered' names a scheme the document does not define.
suggestion: Point test 8 at §4 *buckets* (or move the four-shape enumeration into §2's `unrecognised` paragraph, which is where the gate rule lives, and leave §4 citing §2). Replace 'a numbered decision' with the anchor form the column actually uses, or number §2's decisions so the citation is checkable.

finding: The new 'derives from' column cannot do the job §7 states for it, because its anchors are not addressable. Nine of the twenty cells point at bolded phrases inside a section - '§2 *Default*', '§2 *stamped*', '§2 *next_action*', '§2 *unrecognised*', '§2 table', '§3 *the change rule*', '§4 *buckets*' - which are neither headings nor numbered items, so nothing (tp's own `broken-cross-ref` lint included, since it resolves headings and numbered lists) can tell that a decision moved and its row did not. The column's stated payoff, 'a decision that changes and leaves its row untouched is visible', is then only as reliable as a human diff, which is the mechanism that produced the 14-to-12 lag §7 is repairing. And the bold phrases are themselves editable prose: renaming '**Stamping is symmetric...**' silently orphans row 9b.
suggestion: Give §2, §3 and §4 stable decision labels (D1..Dn as bold literal tokens, or numbered sub-items) and make the column cite those. Then the column is checkable - a `workflow.checks` entry can assert every label appears in exactly one row and every row cites an existing label - and the traceability costs the same twenty cells it costs now.

finding: The replay fixture commits a second copy of data the repository already tracks, to pin a justification rather than a contract. `spec/.tp-review/` is versioned - 568 files are tracked, v0.35.0's and v0.36.0's audit rounds among them - so the ~295 KiB projection §7 specifies duplicates bytes already in the tree. The stated reason ('keeps the test off `spec/.tp-review/`, which is live state for cycles still in flight') holds for an in-flight cycle and not for the two shipped cycles the test reads: v0.35.0's and v0.36.0's round files are frozen by their tags. What the 295 KiB buys is a replay of §2.1's table, which is an argument for a default, not a behaviour tp promises; the predicate itself is already pinned by rows 5-8 on small synthetic rows, and rows 11's numbers are re-derivable from the tracked files at any time.
suggestion: Either read the two shipped cycles' tracked round files directly and pin the immutability with a content hash of those paths, or drop row 11 to the predicate rows (5-8) plus a `consecutive_clean` unit test over a handful of synthetic rounds, and leave §2.1's cells as a measurement with its command recorded. If the projection stays, state what makes 295 KiB the right price for replaying a paragraph.

finding: Three of §7's nineteen `derives from` cells name a clause the spec does not carry under that name, which weakens the mechanism the section was rewritten around ("a decision that changes and leaves its row untouched is visible" only works if the pointer resolves). I checked each cell against the section text. Row 14 cites "§3 *escalation*": the word escalation does not appear anywhere in §3 -- the clause is the paragraph headed "**The refusal is nameable.**". Row 8 cites "§2 *unrecognised*", but the four shapes it asserts ("outside the enum, `null`, absent, or not a string") are enumerated in §4's bucket paragraph, not in §2, which says only "An unrecognised severity is treated as blocking" -- so the row derives from two clauses and names one, and an edit to §4's four shapes would leave row 8 visibly untouched. Row 9b cites "§2 *stamped*" while its content ("the relaxing direction") is the separate paragraph headed "**Stamping is symmetric and the relaxing direction is the one to state.**", which row 9 also points at.
suggestion: Repoint the three cells at the paragraph lead-ins the spec actually carries: row 14 to "§3 *The refusal is nameable*"; row 8 to "§2 *unrecognised* + §4 *buckets*", since the four shapes are §4's; row 9b to "§2 *Stamping is symmetric*". Then add one sentence under the table: "A cell names the bolded lead-in of the paragraph it derives from, verbatim, so the pointer can be resolved by search rather than by reading."

finding: §2.1 spends a paragraph establishing that the table's cells 'are reachable only when the field resolves before round 1 is recorded', because §2 stamps clean at record time and a round recorded before the knob is set 'keeps clean: false for ever'. §7 test 11 says 'replaying ... recorded rounds from committed testdata reproduces the table' and never states that precondition, so the replay's procedure is unpinned in exactly the dimension §2.1 says decides the numbers: an implementer who records round 1 under the default and then sets blocking gets different cells and cannot tell whether the code, the fixture or the procedure is wrong. The row is also unpinned on ordering: §7's closing paragraph lists the projected fields as status, severity, role and item_id, none of which carries a round ordinal, while the assertion is entirely about which round number the streak reaches. Wrong if: test 11 stated that the replay records every round with the field already resolved, and the projection paragraph preserved a round key.
suggestion: Extend test 11's assertion: 'replaying v0.35.0's nine and v0.36.0's thirteen recorded rounds from committed testdata -- **each round recorded with audit_converge_on already resolved, per §2.1** -- reproduces the table ... at audit_clean_rounds: 2'. And extend §7's projection paragraph: 'The projection keeps status, severity, role, item_id and the round's ordinal, one file per round, named audit-round-N.ndjson under a per-cycle directory in the test's own testdata tree.'

finding: §7 row 7's fourth column is `—`, and §7's own opening makes that column the point of the table: "column 4 naming the input that makes it fail", with the stated cost of the old list being that it "went from 14 of 14 writable and 11 discriminating to 12 and 8". A row that declares no falsifying input declares itself non-discriminating, which by §7's own standard is a row that should not be in the list. The input exists and is easy to name -- an implementation that blocks only on the unrecognised bucket, or one that grades `error` by the review ranker (`engine.SeverityRank`, internal/engine/cluster.go:36, which ranks `error` as unknown(4) alongside `warning` and `info`) -- so the em dash is an unfinished cell rather than a true absence. It also loses the one decision in §2 that no other row derives from: "the audit predicate does not reuse the review ranker -- one that did would rank every audit severity as unknown".
suggestion: Fill the cell with the decision it is missing: "| 7 | §2 *Blocking severity is `error`* | `error` blocks under both values, and the predicate does not go through the review ranker | grading the audit row with `engine.SeverityRank`, which ranks `error`, `warning` and `info` alike as unknown |"

finding: §7 test 2's assertion reads 'task override beats project config beats built-in; no CLI or environment layer is asserted, because none exists'. 'is asserted' is ambiguous between 'the test asserts that no such layer exists' and 'the test makes no assertion about such a layer'. One engineer writes a case proving TP_AUDIT_CONVERGE_ON=blocking is ignored; the other writes nothing and calls the row done. The two readings differ in whether the release ships a regression guard on its own precedence, and this repository has already been wrong about this precedence once -- CLAUDE.md records the five-layer claim being removed from this spec at review round 4, and records a sibling spec whose audit spent two rounds unable to verify the top two layers. A row that leaves 'is asserted' undecided is how that error survives into the tests. Wrong if: the cell read 'and a test asserts that TP_AUDIT_CONVERGE_ON and an --audit-converge-on flag are both unrecognised', or 'and no layer beyond these three is tested'.
suggestion: Pick one reading and write it. Recommended, because it guards the error this spec has already made once: 'task override beats project config beats built-in -- three assertions -- and a fourth asserts that TP_AUDIT_CONVERGE_ON=blocking in the environment leaves the resolved value at the layer below it | a resolver reading only the project layer, or an environment layer added silently'.

finding: §7 uses "the corpus" for two different populations two paragraphs apart, and the number an implementer would have to reproduce belongs to the one the fixture does not contain. Row 6 justifies asserting `warning` separately with "158 of the corpus's 360 non-PASS rows"; the paragraph under the table defines the replay fixture as "The 22 recorded round files ... 3,046 rows". I counted both over spec/.tp-review/ with a python3 walk: 158/360 is the whole 90-file audit corpus across every spec; the 22 files of v0.35.0 and v0.36.0 hold 3,046 rows (exactly as stated) of which 133 are non-PASS and 66 are `warning`. So a unit that builds the fixture §7 specifies and then checks row 6's stated reason against it finds 66/133 and cannot tell whether the fixture is wrong, the number is stale, or the two sentences mean different things. Every other measured number in the release reproduced exactly against the tree (v0.35.0's 42 non-PASS as 3/22/17; 2,913 PASS rows all with `severity: null`; 67 outside-enum rows in 15 files across v0.29.0-v0.32.0; the §2.1 table at both `audit_clean_rounds` values), which is what makes this one worth naming rather than the numbers in general.
suggestion: Name the population in row 6: "| 6 | §2 table | `warning` is advisory -- asserted separately from `info`, since it is 158 of the 360 non-`PASS` rows in tp's whole recorded audit corpus, and 66 of the 133 in this release's replay fixture | a predicate that special-cases `info` |" Adding the fixture's own figure makes the row checkable against the artifact the test actually commits.

finding: §7's fourth column is headed 'the input that makes it fail', and its twenty cells hold four different kinds of thing, three of which cannot be run. Actual inputs -- a value to feed the system: row 11 ('recording at 1'). Mutants -- a change to production code to apply and watch fail: rows 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 9b, 10, 14, 15, 16, 17. Descriptions of an inadequate TEST rather than of wrong code: rows 3 ('one test covering one sink while the other path ships ungraded'), 12 ('fencing one file, which leaves the others open'), 18 ('keeping two and deleting seven'). A historical anecdote that cannot be applied at all: row 4 ('v0.31.0 shipped the twin without both and needed v0.31.1'). And row 7's cell is a bare em-dash with no legend, so it is unresolvable between 'no input can falsify this' -- in which case the row is a tautology and a predicate that reports every round unclean passes it -- and 'to be decided'. The column's whole value is that a reader can APPLY the cell and watch the row go red; §7's own framing paragraph says a decision that changes and leaves its row untouched becomes visible, which only holds if the cell is runnable. Wrong if: the header read 'what makes it fail' and a legend defined the em-dash.
suggestion: Rename the column 'the mutant that must fail it' and make every cell applicable. Replace row 4's cell with 'a resolver that emits the field from --extract but accepts any string in validate --project'. Replace row 7's em-dash with 'a predicate that reports every round unclean, which rows 5 and 6 catch only if they assert *clean* under blocking rather than not-clean under all'. Add a legend line under the table: 'Every cell names a change to production code or to a fixture that must make that row's assertion fail. A row whose cell cannot be applied is not yet a test.'

finding: §7's new opening attributes to round 9 a measurement round 9 did not record. "Rounds 8 and 9 both changed §2, §3 and §4 without changing this list, and round 9 measured the cost: the list went from 14 of 14 writable and 11 discriminating to 12 and 8, with four tests demanding the implementation the sections had just rejected." Counted against `spec/.tp-review/0.37.0/review-round-9.ndjson`: the strings '14 of 14', '11 discriminating', '12' and '8' as test-list counts appear nowhere; the only 'writable' figure in the round is a task-decomposability verdict ('THIRTEEN tasks, of which eleven are writable now'), a different subject and a different denominator. The round's recorded rows do flag tests 8, 9, 11, 13 and 14, which is five, not four. The claim is exactly the shape CLAUDE.md's own rule names — a quantifier over a set the author did not enumerate, in a paragraph whose whole point is that an unmaintained list is measurable — and unlike the counts in §1, §2 and §7 test 6, which all verify exactly against the corpus, this one has no artifact behind it.
suggestion: Either bind the numbers to the artifact (name the round file and the rule by which a test counts as writable/discriminating, so the figures can be re-derived) or delete the sentence and keep the decision it introduces: the derivation column exists so a changed decision with an untouched row is visible.

finding: The refusal identifies the field twice and row 14 pins both. `--decision audit-converge-on` is the machine-readable identification, and the bespoke message is the human-readable one; the reason §3 gives for not reusing the existing message is that the generic one 'interpolates the field name and so passes a substring check' - a test-discrimination problem, not something the operator reading the escalation lacks. Under `tp run` the operator sees the escalation record, which already carries the decision name and `--evidence`.
suggestion: Either drop the bespoke message and let row 14 discriminate on the recorded `--decision` value (which the generic message cannot fake), or say what the operator learns from the new message that the decision name plus the evidence text does not tell them. One channel per fact keeps the enum growth paying for itself as further fields are fenced.

finding: The `--compact` retention is asserted by analogy to a payload that does not resemble this one. The twin's `nonblocking_open` is a single integer on `--record`/`--status`, and REFERENCE.md §8.4 keeps it because its bare presence is the accepted-open signal. `by_severity` is a map on `tp audit --merge`, a payload that already carries `findings` (the non-PASS count) and `by_status` unconditionally, and whose only other map, `overlap_report`, is stripped under `--compact` as explanatory. So on this command presence signals nothing the compact payload does not already carry, and the imported rationale does not transfer. The map may still be worth keeping - the mix is what an agent acts on - but that argument has not been made.
suggestion: Justify the retention on this payload: state that under `--compact` the breakdown is what tells an agent whether the accepted rows are `warning` or `info`, which `findings` and `by_status` cannot, and reconcile it explicitly with `overlap_report` being stripped from the same summary. Row 16 then pins a decision rather than an inherited one.

finding: §6a's count is prose that has been wrong twice and is re-litigated every round ('The count is three because earlier drafts said one and then two'), while what a decomposer needs is the set, not the number - and the set is derivable by running: every assertion that reddens when the sentence and `engine.DivergenceHint` change. A number defended by its own drafting history is the shape this repo has repeatedly measured as unstable, and each round spends findings re-counting it.
suggestion: State the membership rule rather than the cardinality - 'every shipped assertion that reddens when the counted-every-non-PASS-row sentence changes; run the gate to enumerate them' - and let the task's acceptance list the sites it actually found. The count then cannot be wrong in the next round, because the spec no longer asserts one.

finding: Row 7 ("§2 table | `error` blocks") has an em dash in "the input that makes it fail". The table's whole argument is that the derivation and the falsifying input are what keep a row honest — §7's preamble measures round 9's list as "12 [writable] and 8 [discriminating]" and calls the column the fix. A row with no falsifying input is a row that certifies itself, which is the state the column was added to make visible, and it is visible here only as punctuation.
suggestion: Fill it: "a predicate that treats `error` as advisory", or "a `blocking` predicate that returns clean for any round, which rows 5 and 6 also pass". If no input can discriminate row 7 from rows 5 and 6, fold it into them rather than carrying a row the column cannot support.

finding: The rewritten test table numbers its rows 1-19 but carries 20 rows, because 9b sits between 9 and 10. Every cross-reference to a test in this cycle is by number ('§7 test 11', 'test 13'), and §5/§6/§2 use the same form for cross-spec pointers, so a table whose ids are not a contiguous integer sequence makes 'test N' ambiguous between position and label, and makes a later renumber silent. §6a's own history in this file is the precedent: three earlier rounds recorded pointers to '§5 test 12' and '§5 test 9' that resolved to the wrong row after a list changed length.
suggestion: Renumber the rows 1-20 and let the derivation column carry the pairing that 9/9b was expressing (both cite §2 *stamped*), so an id is a position and a pointer cannot drift.

finding: §2's clearest new observable -- 'Under blocking a round can record clean: true beside a non-zero open, and that is correct' -- sits on §7's 'Not tested here, named so the absence is deliberate' list, justified as 'severity-blind by §2's boundary; spec/0.46.0.md §8 owns changing that'. §8 owns CHANGING the streaks. It does not own asserting that THIS release preserves them while making clean diverge from open for the first time in tp's history, which is the release's whole behavioural signature. The exclusion therefore defers a regression assertion under cover of deferring a feature, and it is the cheapest assertion available: test 10 already builds the fixture that produces it. Wrong if: §7's exclusion paragraph said the clean/open pairing is asserted here and only the future severity-awareness deferred.
suggestion: Move the pairing off the exclusion list and into the table: '| 10b | §2 *boundary* | under blocking, one round reports clean: true and a non-zero role_streaks[].open on the same payload, and spec_coverage_clean_rounds counts that round | making the streaks severity-aware, which zeroes open and hides the divergence |'. Keep the exclusion paragraph for the future change only, rewording it to 'making the streaks severity-aware is deferred; that they stay severity-blind here is test 10b.'

finding: §7's new preamble is five lines of round-9 postmortem with measured cycle numbers ('14 of 14 writable and 11 discriminating to 12 and 8') sitting above the table. It sits under a 16-line blockquote of round-7 postmortem at the top of the same file, and §2 carries three more 'an earlier draft' paragraphs. None of it is a decision to build; all of it is re-read by every future round, by every role's prompt (the emitted prompt carries the section text), and by the decomposer. The counts are also the class this repo has recorded as rotting fastest - a measured constant whose recount nobody is obliged to redo.
suggestion: Keep the one sentence that states the rule ('a decision that changes and leaves its row untouched is visible') and move the postmortem numbers to the cycle's own notes or to the task acceptance where the column is built. The rule is what the reader must act on; the history is what the reader pays for.
